newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to free 38 Indian children ahead of talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to free 38 Indian children ahead of talks.

text.p: Pakistan, in a goodwill gesture ahead of peace talks with India this month, said on Saturday it was releasing 38 children who were among people detained aboard Indian fishing boats caught in Pakistani waters.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman said the Indian High Commission in Islamabad had been asked to arrange for the repatriation of the children, now in the care of the private Karachi-based Edhi Welfare Trust organisation.
"This is a unilateral gesture which we hope will help the atmosphere in the talks and also lead to the release of all the boats and crew on both sides," the spokesman said.
The secretaries, or top civil servants, of the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministries are due to meet in New Delhi from March 28 to 31 to revive a dialogue stalled since January 1994.
The spokesman said India and Pakistan each held more than 100 of each other's nationals detained on fishing boats that had strayed into the territorial waters of the rival neighbours.

Normally they are freed on a reciprocal basis, but the spokesman said India had created some new problems in this process by saying not all the boats it held were fishing boats because some had been found carrying cargo.
Indian diplomats could not immediately be reached for comment.
Pakistani social worker Abdus Sattar Edhi said he would give $100 and clothes to each of the Indian children, now aged 10 to 16, who have been detained for the past three years.

Edhi, who runs a volunteer network of ambulance and other emergency services throughout Pakistan, told Reuters he had been looking after the young detainees at the Edhi Village for children, about 70 km (44 miles) northeast of Karachi.

"The children were free to move within the village and there was no police guard to keep an eye on them," he said. "I never considered them as prisoners. They were allowed to celebrate festivals including Diwali and Holi according to their own religion and customs. They were also provided books in Hindi."
Edhi, a Moslem who migrated from India in 1947, said he did not believe children should be detained indefinitely.
"India should reciprocate the gesture and release Pakistanis under detention in that country," he said.
